quotes.quote: The axons of the ganglion cells pass over the inner surface of the retina and converge towards the posterior pole of the eye, where they pierce through foramina in the sclera and then constitute the optic nerve.

Within the optic chiasm a partial decussation takes place: fibres from the nasal halves of the retinae, including the projection of the monocular visual field, cross to the opposite side; those from the temporal halves of the retinas remain uncrossed
After this partial decussation, the axons of the retinal ganglion cells continue without interruption behind the chiasm as the two diverging optic tracts.
These arch around the lateral sides of the diencephalon until they reach the lateral geniculate bodies, where most of their fibres terminate.
Layer M1 and layers P4 and P6 receive fibres from the contralateral eye, and layer M2 and layers P3 and P5 receive fibres from the ipsilateral eye
The efferent fibres of the lateral geniculate body constitute the optic radiation or geniculocalcarine tract, which terminates in the primary visual cortex.
The upper quadrant of the visual field is represented in the contralateral V1 cortex of the lower bank of the calcarine sulcus
the lower quadrant is represented in the upper bank of this sulcus
The fovea, i.e. the retinal areas concerned with central vision, projects to a relatively large area in the posterior part of the primary visual cortex.
The nasal periphery of the retina, concerned with the temporal, monocular periphery of the visual field, projects to the extreme anterior part of the visual cortex

some fibres continue in a mediocaudal direction and pass via the brachium of the superior colliculus to the superior colliculus, the pretectal region and the terminal nuclei of the accessory optic system
Several retinocortical pathways to nonprimary visual areas avoid the lateral geniculate body and synapse in the superior colliculus and the pulvinar.
The retinogeniculocortical projection and the extrageniculate and extrastriate visual pathways.

The axons of the type 1 cells of the spiral ganglion bifurcate in the centre of the ventral cochlear nucleus, dividing it into the anterior and posterior ventral nucleus, and distribute in a tonotopical manner to both the dorsal and the ventral cochlear nuclei
The trapezoid body crosses in the ventral part of the tegmentum.

The terminations of the axons of the globular bushy cells in the central portion of the ventral cochlear nucleus envelop the cells of the contralateral nucleus of the trapezoid body with their calyces

The spherical bushy cells located in the anterior portion of the ventral cochlear nucleus project to the ipsilateral lateral superior olivary nucleus and to the medial superior olivary nucleus of both sides
The medial superior olive receives a projection to its lateral half from the ipsilateral cochlear nuclei and to its medial half from the contralateral side.
The lateral superior olive receives tonotopically arranged projections from the ipsilateral and contralateral cochlear nuclei.

The highly specific spatial organization of afferents to cells in the medial superior olivary nucleus has to do with its role in interpreting interaural time differences, which are maximal at low frequencies.
For the localization of sound, interaural level differences, which are maximal at high frequencies, are encoded in the lateral superior olive

Both superior olivary nuclei project in turn to the dorsal nucleus of the lateral lemniscus and the inferior colliculus; the projection of the medial superior olive is an ipsilateral one, and the projections of the lateral superior olive are bilateral
The brachium of the inferior colliculus, a prominent bundle visible on the surface of the midbrain, connects the inferior colliculus with the medial geniculate body
The final link in the auditory system is formed by the auditory radiation through which the medial geniculate body is connected with the superior temporal cortex.
Passing laterally, this radiation traverses the sublenticular portion of the internal capsule.
The primary auditory cortex (known as its core area) corresponds roughly to the transverse gyrus of Heschl.
The final link in this descending system is formed by the olivocochlear bundle, which originates from the superior olivary complex.
The medial system originates from large periolivary neurons located medial to the superior olives (medial nucleus of the trapezoid body).
Its coarse axons project bilaterally to the cochlea, where they form large synaptic terminals at the base of the outer hair cells
Most fibres of the lateral olivocochlear system take their origin from small neurons located within the lateral superior olive
The crossed projection of the small neurons is topically organized; shell cells project diffusely over the entire length of the ipsilateral cochlea
The first-order elements are bipolar neurons, the somata of which constitute the vestibular ganglion, located in the internal auditory meatus.
It comprises four cell masses, the superior, lateral, medial and descending (or inferior) vestibular nuclei
Vestibular rootfibres reach the cerebellum via the superior vestibular nucleus.
Primary vestibular afferents reach the cerebellum through the juxtarestiform body.
The cerebellovestibular fibres arise from Purkinje cells located in the flocculonodular lobe, the uvula and the anterior vermis, and from the fastigial nucleus
Purkinje cells of the vestibulocerebellum (nodulus and adjoining uvula, flocculus and ventral paraflocculus) project to the other vestibular nuclei and group Y.
The lateral vestibulospinal tract takes its origin from the lateral vestibular nucleus.
The main component of the lateral vestibulospinal tract descends to lumbar levels.

The lateral vestibulospinal tract is an uncrossed pathway from the lateral vestibular nucleus located lateral to the MLF in the centre of the bulbar reticular formation, that descends along the entire spinal cord
Two other fibre systems, corresponding to the medial and the crossed vestibulospinal tracts, descend in or adjacent to the MLF
The medial vestibulospinal tract is located ipsilaterally in the dorsolateral bulbar MLF and consists of mediumsized and small fibres.
Fibres of the crossed vestibulospinal tract decussate at their level of origin and become located next to the midline in the MLF.
The three-neuron arc of the vestibulo-ocular reflex connecting the semicircular canals with the extraocular muscles.

Horizontal canal fibres terminate on two groups of excitatory neurons located in the MVmc, projecting to the contralateral abducens nucleus and the ipsilateral medial rectus pool of motoneurons in the nucleus of the oculomotor nerve
However, there is evidence that cells located within the superior, medial and inferior vestibular nuclei give rise to fibres that terminate in the thalamus.
They decussate in the isthmus region and pass diffusely through the midbrain tegmentum and the fields of Forel to terminate in the thalamus.

In primates the vestibulothalamic fibres terminate bilaterally in the shell surrounding the ventral posterior nuclei (ventral posterior superior nucleus, VPS, and ventral posterior inferior nucleus, VPI)
Similar vestibular cortical areas also were localized in the human brain using fMRI after bilateral galvanic stimulation of the labyrinth

It should be noted that the vestibular nerve, in addition to afferent fibres, also carries a number of efferent fibres.

quotes.quote: It seems that the vestibular cortex has the form of an extensive network rather than a discrete, limited, and well-demarcated cortical location.

Special visceral afferents that innervate taste buds in the fungiform papillae of the anterior half of the tongue and foliate papillae along its lateral edges course in the chorda tympani and the intermediate nerve, usually included with the facial nerve.
Taste buds of the palate and the pharynx are innervated by the vagus nerve.

The nucleus of the solitary tract can be subdivided into a rostral gustatory portion, which receives gustatory afferents from the facial, glossopharyngeal and vagal nerves, and a caudal portion, which receives general visceral afferents from these nerves.
The first relay for taste is located in the nucleus of the solitary tract in the lower brain stem.
The rostral, gustatory portion of the solitary nucleus gives rise to an uncrossed ascending pathway terminating in the caudal half of the parvocellular VPM

The uncrossed gustatory pathway, from the rostral solitary nucleus to the caudal half of the parvocellular medial ventroposterior nucleus of the thalamus (VPp), ascends near the dorsal trigeminothalamic tract.
Most of these connections, with the exception of the pathway for taste, are crossed.
The parvocellular VPM projects to the gustatory cortex, located in the rostral, granular cortex of the insula and the inner frontal operculum
VPp projects to the rostral insula and the frontal operculum, and to the base of the postcentral gyrus.

Secondary olfactory fibres originating from the olfactory bulb pass by way of the lateral olfactory tract to the amygdala, where they terminate mainly in the cortical nucleus
The lateral olfactory stria carries secondary olfactory fibres to the cortical and medial amygdaloid nuclei.
The amygdala receives a direct projection from the olfactory bulb, which terminates mainly in the cortical nucleus
Impulses carrying information from all sense organs except olfactory terminate in particular thalamic nuclei, where they are projected to specific cortical areas by thalamic relay cells
After having distributed fibres to the anterior olfactory nucleus and the olfactory tubercle, the entire secondary olfactory projection enters the lateral olfactory stria
Following that stria, the fibres reach the prepiriform, periamygdaloid and entorhinal cortices and the cortical amygdaloid nucleus, where they terminate

also receive direct projections from the olfactory bulb

Thus it has been established that the prepiriform cortex distributes fibres to the basolateral complex and that the entorhinal cortex projects to the central, basolateral and cortical nuclei
